title: The AI bugpocalypse is here. Now what? - Jack Cable, Corridor

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is security, guardrails, and governance of AI coding systems—vulnerability discovery, guardrails on coding agents, export controls, and Congressional policy recommendations. The talk addresses security operations and defense in the context of AI coding assistants like Cursor and Claude Code. The talk spans development (AI writing code), evaluation (Backsbench vulnerability benchmarks), deployment (guardrails and AI code review), and governance (policy and Congressional testimony). The talk assumes familiarity with vulnerability classes, memory safety, and AI policy, targeting security professionals and engineers. This is a conference talk at the AI Engineer conference. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Jack Cable frames the AI bug apocalypse as a dual-shift: frontier models are rapidly improving at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, while AI coding tools are scaling faster than any software category in history—with ~84% of developers and 30-40% of companies already adopting them, and coding agents becoming increasingly autonomous. This expands attack surfaces just as adversaries gain automated tooling across the full attack chain. Drawing on his CISA secure-by-design work, Cable emphasizes that the vulnerabilities AI models find are not novel—they are basic, decades-old classes like buffer overflows, cross-site scripting, and SQL injection, all cataloged in MITRE's top exploited vulnerability classes. This is good news: we already know how to prevent entire classes. Memory-safe languages (Rust, Go) can eliminate 60-70% of vulnerabilities in memory-unsafe language codebases. Google's Android data shows memory safety vulnerabilities dropping from ~75% (2019) to ~30% (2022) simply by writing new code in Rust. Cable argues for strategic one-time rewrites of critical libraries rather than perpetual whack-a-mole patching, since language-level guarantees hold even as models get smarter. On the flip side, AI coding tools themselves introduce vulnerabilities: the Backsbench benchmark shows even the best models introduce vulnerabilities 20-40% of the time. These failures are often contextual—authorization bugs requiring deep business-logic understanding that models lack. Cable predicts that within 6-12 months, the majority of shipped code will be AI-reviewed rather than human-reviewed, making guardrails on coding agents essential so security is not a blocker for acceleration. Corridor's approach focuses on preventing vulnerabilities before the pull request and giving security teams visibility into AI tool usage. On policy, Cable testified before Congress and co-signed a letter urging the White House to lift export controls on frontier models, arguing that defender benefits outweigh risks—especially as open-weight models close the gap with closed-weight models via distillation attacks. His three Congressional recommendations: prevent vulnerabilities in new code going forward, harden the open-source foundation (which serves as a proving ground for adversaries), and foster an ecosystem of American-made open-weight models for competitiveness and fine-tuning flexibility. He closes by stressing the importance of returning to fundamental controls that protect against vulnerabilities discoverable by any model, present or future.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Jack Cable introduces himself as Co-Founder and CEO of Corridor (securing AI coding), former CISA senior technical advisor, and ethical hacker who ranked in the top 100 on HackerOne in high school. He frames the talk around the AI bug apocalypse: frontier models finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in production software at scale.

sections.title: AI Coding Adoption and Growing Attack Surface
sections.summary: Cable sets the stage: AI coding tools (Cursor, Copilot) are scaling faster than any software category. ~84% of developers and 30-40% of companies were using them, with increasing autonomy—agents running in the background from Slack. Both sides of the equation are shifting: models find vulnerabilities better, and attack surfaces grow as AI becomes the default code writer.

sections.title: Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Attack Chain
sections.summary: Cable references Anthropic's Mythos chart showing rapid model advancement in autonomous attack chain execution. Adversaries will automate every part of the attack process, not just discovery. The core question becomes: how can defenders use the same AI techniques to harden systems, ensuring models don't introduce exponentially more vulnerabilities over time?

sections.title: Secure by Design and Common Vulnerability Classes
sections.summary: Cable draws on his CISA secure-by-design paper (March 2023). MITRE's top exploited vulnerability classes from CISA's KEV catalog are all basic, decades-old types (e.g., buffer overflows at #2). The key insight: vulnerabilities AI models find aren't novel classes—we've known how to prevent them at scale for decades.

sections.title: Memory-Safe Languages as Strategic Prevention
sections.summary: Cable advocates for memory-safe languages (Rust, Go) as a fundamental fix: 60-70% of vulnerabilities in memory-unsafe language products are preventable. Google Android data shows memory safety vulnerabilities dropping from ~75% (2019) to ~30% (2022) just from writing new code in Rust. He argues for one-time rewrites of critical libraries versus perpetual whack-a-mole patching, since language guarantees hold even as models improve.

sections.title: AI Models Introducing Vulnerabilities
sections.summary: Cable addresses the flip side: AI coding tools introduce vulnerabilities. An Opus 46 model introduced a smart contract vulnerability leading to millions stolen. The Backsbench benchmark (ETH Zurich, UC Berkeley) shows even the best models introduce vulnerabilities 20-40% of the time. Failures are increasingly contextual—authorization bugs requiring business-logic understanding that models lack because they aren't trained on proprietary company threat models.

sections.title: AI Code Review and Guardrails for Autonomous Development
sections.summary: Cable describes the autonomy ladder: autocomplete to synchronous agents (Cursor, Claude Code) to autonomous agents working hours at a time, with AI code review as the next step. He predicts within 6-12 months the majority of shipped code will be AI-reviewed, since code review is becoming the bottleneck. Corridor's approach centers on preventing vulnerabilities before the pull request and giving security teams visibility into AI tool usage. Cable argues security cannot be the blocker for acceleration—organizations should enable coding agents with guardrails, not restrict them.

sections.title: Policy Perspective: Export Controls and Open-Weight Models
sections.summary: Cable discusses policy implications, including a letter led by Mikayla Gyalcsamis urging the White House to lift export controls on Mythos and Fable models. He argues defender benefits far outweigh risks for these dual-use models. Anthropic has built safeguards into the Fable release skewing toward defenders. However, open-weight models are rapidly closing the gap with closed-weight models via distillation attacks, meaning adversaries already have access to powerful models. Cable advocates for rapidly getting defensive capabilities into defenders' hands through wider model availability.

sections.title: Congressional Testimony and Recommendations
sections.summary: Cable testified before US Congress on risks of frontier models and AI coding. His recommendations: (1) prevent vulnerabilities in new code going forward, ensuring security isn't left behind as development accelerates; (2) harden the open-source foundation, since open-source software is the proving ground for adversaries testing models and finding novel vulnerabilities; and (3) pursue systemic rewrites rather than one-off patches to fundamentally reduce vulnerability risk. Both government and private companies share responsibility for shoring up open-source.

sections.title: Fostering American Open-Weight Models and Conclusion
sections.summary: Cable's third recommendation is to foster an ecosystem of American-made open-weight models, essential for competitiveness since companies need fine-tuning capabilities only open-weight models provide. He closes by emphasizing the rapidly evolving space makes it all the more important to return to fundamental controls that protect against vulnerabilities discoverable by any model, present or future, and to use these models to make systems more resilient.
